title: Notification System
scopeHtml: Scope: Strategy per channel, templates, retry with backoff and dead letter, async delivery and bulkheads, idempotency, priorities and fallback.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Design a notification system that sends a message to a user over email, SMS and push, using templates, and retries when a provider fails.

Clarify first: which channels? Does the user choose channels (opt-in)? Are messages templated with variables? What happens after retries are exhausted? Is delivery synchronous or fire-and-forget? Priority levels, rate limits and scheduling are follow-ups. (Here: 3 channels, per-user opt-in, {{placeholder}} templates, 3 attempts with exponential backoff, a dead-letter list, async option.)

Worked example. 2M users get a "flash sale" push at 12:00. At 20,000 sends/s that takes 100 s, and if FCM errors 1% of the time, 20,000 messages need a retry. With a 100 ms base backoff, up to 3 attempts, the retries add about 300 ms of waiting per failing message, which must not block healthy ones.

Industry examples. Amazon SES / SNS, Twilio (SMS), Firebase Cloud Messaging and APNs (push), SendGrid; internally Uber and Airbnb run a central notification platform with templates, preferences, rate caps and a queue (Kafka or SQS) between producers and channel workers.

Everyday analogy. A post office with three counters (letter, telegram, courier). You hand over the message once; the clerk picks the counters you subscribed to and tries again if the courier is out.

Common interview traps.

  • Coupling business code to a provider (new TwilioClient() in the order service).
  • Not asking about user preferences and unsubscribe, which are legal requirements for marketing mail.
  • Ignoring failure: "we just call the API" has no answer to the provider being down.

notes.title: Core entities
notes.html:
• ChannelType (EMAIL, SMS, PUSH): enum.
  • User: id, addresses (email, phone, device token), opted-in channels.
  • Message: channel, destination, rendered body. The unit we send and retry.
  • Channel (interface): send(Message); one class per provider.
  • TemplateEngine: name plus variables to body text.
  • RetryPolicy: max attempts, base delay, cap.
  • NotificationService: orchestrates: render once, fan out to wanted + opted-in channels, retry each independently, dead-letter on exhaustion.

Decision gravity. Channel as an interface is the one-way door: ten services will depend on it. Concrete providers behind it are cheap to swap (switching Twilio for Vonage is one class). Rendering once and fanning out means the body is identical across retries.

Everyday analogy. The mail room clerk: reads the letter once, photocopies it per counter, and keeps a "could not deliver" tray.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting retry logic inside each channel class (duplicated). Keep it in the service or a decorator.
  • Making User know about providers.

How to read it. The service owns a map from type to channel, so adding WhatsApp is: add enum value, write one class, register it. Nothing else changes (Open/Closed).

Common interview traps.

  • A giant if (type == EMAIL) ... else if (type == SMS) in the service.
  • Forgetting Sleeper; without it your retry test sleeps for real seconds.

notes.title: Key patterns
notes.html:
• Strategy (Channel): each provider is an interchangeable algorithm for "deliver this message". Why: add or swap channels without touching the service. Alternative: subclass per notification type (explodes: EmailOrderShipped, SmsOrderShipped, ...). Breaks when channels need very different payloads (rich push vs plain SMS); then introduce a per-channel template variant. Reversible.
  • Template Method / simple engine: rendering separated from delivery, so marketing can edit text without a deploy. Fail fast on a missing variable: sending "Hi {{name}}" to a customer is worse than not sending.
  • Retry with exponential backoff: delay = base * 2^(attempt-1), capped: 100, 200, 400 ms ... Add jitter in production so thousands of failures do not retry in lockstep (thundering herd).
  • Dead-letter queue: failed messages are parked for inspection and replay instead of lost. Kafka/SQS offer it natively.
  • Observer (extension): delivery-status listeners (analytics, audit).

Industry examples. AWS SDKs and gRPC retry with exponential backoff plus jitter; SQS has a redrive policy to a dead-letter queue after maxReceiveCount.

Everyday analogy. Redialling a busy friend: wait a bit longer each time, and after three tries leave a note instead.

Common interview traps.

  • Retrying non-retryable errors (invalid phone number, 400). Retry only transient failures (timeouts, 5xx, 429).
  • Retrying without idempotency: the user may get the SMS twice. Send an idempotency key to the provider where supported.

notes.title: Code
notes.html:
Full runnable file Main.java (service, channels, template engine, retry, async wrapper and a test):

import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

enum ChannelType { EMAIL, SMS, PUSH }

class User {
    final String id, email, phone, deviceToken;
    final Set<ChannelType> optedIn;
    User(String id, String email, String phone, String deviceToken, Set<ChannelType> optedIn) {
        this.id = id; this.email = email; this.phone = phone; this.deviceToken = deviceToken; this.optedIn = optedIn;
    }
    String addressFor(ChannelType t) {
        switch (t) { case EMAIL: return email; case SMS: return phone; default: return deviceToken; }
    }
}

class Message {
    final ChannelType channel; final String to, body;
    Message(ChannelType channel, String to, String body) { this.channel = channel; this.to = to; this.body = body; }
}

/** Strategy: one implementation per provider (SES, Twilio, FCM...). Throws on failure. */
interface Channel {
    ChannelType type();
    void send(Message m) throws Exception;
}

/** Templates are plain text with {{placeholders}}. Missing variable = fail fast, never ship "{{name}}". */
class TemplateEngine {
    private final Map<String, String> templates = new HashMap<>();
    void register(String name, String text) { templates.put(name, text); }
    String render(String name, Map<String, String> vars) {
        String t = templates.get(name);
        if (t == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("no template " + name);
        for (Map.Entry<String, String> e : vars.entrySet()) t = t.replace("{{" + e.getKey() + "}}", e.getValue());
        if (t.contains("{{")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unfilled placeholder in: " + t);
        return t;
    }
}

/** Exponential backoff: base * 2^(attempt-1), capped. Sleeper is injectable so tests do not wait. */
class RetryPolicy {
    final int maxAttempts; final long baseMs, capMs;
    RetryPolicy(int maxAttempts, long baseMs, long capMs) { this.maxAttempts = maxAttempts; this.baseMs = baseMs; this.capMs = capMs; }
    long delayMs(int attempt) { return Math.min(capMs, baseMs << (attempt - 1)); }
}

interface Sleeper { void sleep(long ms) throws InterruptedException; }

class NotificationService {
    private final Map<ChannelType, Channel> channels = new EnumMap<>(ChannelType.class);
    private final TemplateEngine templates; private final RetryPolicy retry; private final Sleeper sleeper;
    final List<Message> deadLetter = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

    NotificationService(List<Channel> cs, TemplateEngine templates, RetryPolicy retry, Sleeper sleeper) {
        for (Channel c : cs) channels.put(c.type(), c);
        this.templates = templates; this.retry = retry; this.sleeper = sleeper;
    }

    /** Fan-out to every channel the user opted into. One channel failing must not block the others. */
    Map<ChannelType, Boolean> notify(User u, String template, Map<String, String> vars, Set<ChannelType> wanted) {
        String body = templates.render(template, vars);
        Map<ChannelType, Boolean> result = new EnumMap<>(ChannelType.class);
        for (ChannelType t : wanted) {
            if (!u.optedIn.contains(t) || !channels.containsKey(t)) continue;
            result.put(t, deliver(new Message(t, u.addressFor(t), body)));
        }
        return result;
    }

    private boolean deliver(Message m) {
        Channel c = channels.get(m.channel);
        for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= retry.maxAttempts; attempt++) {
            try { c.send(m); return true; }
            catch (Exception e) {
                if (attempt == retry.maxAttempts) break;
                try { sleeper.sleep(retry.delayMs(attempt)); }
                catch (InterruptedException ie) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); break; }
            }
        }
        deadLetter.add(m);                    // park it for manual replay / alerting
        return false;
    }
}

/** Concurrency: run each notify on a pool so a slow SMS provider does not block the caller. */
class AsyncNotifier implements AutoCloseable {
    private final NotificationService svc; private final ExecutorService pool;
    AsyncNotifier(NotificationService svc, int threads) { this.svc = svc; this.pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads); }
    Future<Map<ChannelType, Boolean>> notify(User u, String tpl, Map<String, String> v, Set<ChannelType> w) {
        return pool.submit(() -> svc.notify(u, tpl, v, w));
    }
    public void close() { pool.shutdown(); }
}

public class Main {
    static class FakeChannel implements Channel {
        final ChannelType type; final AtomicInteger failuresLeft; final AtomicInteger sent = new AtomicInteger();
        FakeChannel(ChannelType type, int failFirst) { this.type = type; this.failuresLeft = new AtomicInteger(failFirst); }
        public ChannelType type() { return type; }
        public void send(Message m) throws Exception {
            if (failuresLeft.getAndDecrement() > 0) throw new Exception("provider down");
            sent.incrementAndGet();
        }
    }
    static void check(boolean c, String msg) { if (!c) throw new AssertionError(msg); }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        TemplateEngine tpl = new TemplateEngine();
        tpl.register("order_shipped", "Hi {{name}}, order {{orderId}} has shipped.");
        FakeChannel email = new FakeChannel(ChannelType.EMAIL, 2);   // fails twice then works
        FakeChannel sms = new FakeChannel(ChannelType.SMS, 99);      // always fails
        FakeChannel push = new FakeChannel(ChannelType.PUSH, 0);
        List<Long> slept = new ArrayList<>();
        NotificationService svc = new NotificationService(List.of(email, sms, push), tpl,
                new RetryPolicy(3, 100, 1000), slept::add);
        User u = new User("u1", "a@x.com", "+911", "tok", EnumSet.of(ChannelType.EMAIL, ChannelType.SMS, ChannelType.PUSH));
        Map<String, String> vars = Map.of("name", "Asha", "orderId", "42");

        Map<ChannelType, Boolean> r = svc.notify(u, "order_shipped", vars, EnumSet.allOf(ChannelType.class));
        check(r.get(ChannelType.EMAIL) && !r.get(ChannelType.SMS) && r.get(ChannelType.PUSH), "per-channel result");
        check(slept.equals(List.of(100L, 200L, 100L, 200L)), "backoff 100,200 for email and again for sms: " + slept);
        check(svc.deadLetter.size() == 1, "sms in dead letter");

        boolean threw = false;
        try { svc.notify(u, "order_shipped", Map.of("name", "A"), EnumSet.of(ChannelType.PUSH)); }
        catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { threw = true; }
        check(threw, "missing variable rejected");

        try (AsyncNotifier async = new AsyncNotifier(svc, 4)) {
            List<Future<Map<ChannelType, Boolean>>> fs = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int i = 0; i < 50; i++) fs.add(async.notify(u, "order_shipped", vars, EnumSet.of(ChannelType.PUSH)));
            for (Future<?> f : fs) f.get();
        }
        check(push.sent.get() == 51, "51 pushes, got " + push.sent.get());
        System.out.println("P8 OK");
    }
}

The core in Kotlin:

enum class ChannelType { EMAIL, SMS, PUSH }
data class Message(val channel: ChannelType, val to: String, val body: String)

interface Channel { val type: ChannelType; fun send(m: Message) } // throws on failure

class RetryPolicy(val maxAttempts: Int, val baseMs: Long, val capMs: Long) {
    fun delayMs(attempt: Int) = minOf(capMs, baseMs shl (attempt - 1))
}

class NotificationService(
    channels: List<Channel>,
    private val render: (String, Map<String, String>) -> String,
    private val retry: RetryPolicy,
    private val sleep: (Long) -> Unit = Thread::sleep,
) {
    private val byType = channels.associateBy { it.type }
    val deadLetter = java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList<Message>()

    fun notify(optedIn: Set<ChannelType>, addr: (ChannelType) -> String,
               tpl: String, vars: Map<String, String>, wanted: Set<ChannelType>): Map<ChannelType, Boolean> {
        val body = render(tpl, vars)                       // render once
        return wanted.filter { it in optedIn && it in byType }
            .associateWith { deliver(Message(it, addr(it), body)) }
    }

    private fun deliver(m: Message): Boolean {
        for (attempt in 1..retry.maxAttempts) {
            try { byType.getValue(m.channel).send(m); return true }
            catch (e: Exception) { if (attempt < retry.maxAttempts) sleep(retry.delayMs(attempt)) }
        }
        deadLetter += m
        return false
    }
}

Walk-through. Email fails twice then succeeds: delays 100 ms and 200 ms, result true. SMS always fails: it sleeps 100 and 200 ms (no sleep after the last attempt), lands in deadLetter, result false. Push succeeds first time. One channel failing never blocks another because each deliver is independent.

Common interview traps.

  • Sleeping after the final failed attempt (wasted wait).
  • Letting one exception escape the loop and abort the other channels.
  • Using double for delays with shifts; keep long and cap to avoid overflow at high attempt counts.

notes.title: Run and test
notes.html:
javac Main.java && java -ea Main
# prints: P8 OK

The test uses FakeChannel objects that fail a set number of times, and a Sleeper that records delays instead of waiting. It asserts: per-channel results (email true, sms false, push true); recorded backoff 100, 200, 100, 200; one dead-lettered message; a template with a missing variable is rejected; and 50 async pushes all arrive (51 total).

Common interview traps.

  • Real network calls in unit tests. Inject fakes.
  • No test for the "all attempts failed" path, where most bugs live.

notes.title: Concurrency
notes.html:
In production this is never a synchronous method on the request thread. The request thread should only enqueue.

  • Thread pool (shown): AsyncNotifier runs notify on a fixed pool. Pool size is about requestsPerSec * avgLatencySec (Little's law): 2,000 sends/s at 150 ms each needs about 300 threads, or far fewer with async HTTP clients.
  • State is thread-safe: the channel map is read-only after construction; deadLetter is a CopyOnWriteArrayList (rarely written, fine; for heavy failure rates use a ConcurrentLinkedQueue); counters use AtomicInteger.
  • Per-channel isolation (bulkhead): a separate pool or queue per channel, so a slow SMS provider cannot starve push. Circuit breaker (Resilience4j, Hystrix): after N consecutive failures stop calling the provider for 30 s and send straight to the retry queue.
  • Ordering and duplicates: with at-least-once queues you get duplicates; dedupe with a notificationId stored in Redis SETNX with a TTL (for example 24 h).
  • Blocking retries waste threads. Sleeping inside a worker pins a thread. At scale, re-enqueue with a delay (SQS delay seconds, Kafka retry topics retry-1m, retry-5m) instead.

Incident pattern. A provider degrades from 100 ms to 10 s responses; the thread pool fills with waiting calls and every channel stalls. Symptom: queue lag climbs and thread-pool active count sits at max. Fix: timeouts on every provider call (for example 2 s), bulkheads, circuit breaker.

Decision gravity. Synchronous-first is reversible; adding a queue changes the contract from "sent" to "accepted", a one-way door for API callers, so decide early.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant: the waiter (API) writes the order on a ticket (queue) and returns to the floor; separate kitchen stations (workers) cook without the waiter standing there.

Common interview traps.

  • Retrying in the request thread (user waits 30 s).
  • Unbounded queues that hide a stuck provider until memory runs out.
  • No timeouts: a hung socket retries forever.

notes.title: Follow-ups
notes.html:
• Priorities: OTPs must jump ahead of marketing (separate queues or priority topics).
  • Rate limiting per user and per provider: reuse the token bucket from the Rate limiter problem (P11).
  • Scheduling and quiet hours: delay queue; respect user time zone.
  • Delivery tracking: provider webhooks update status (sent, delivered, bounced); unsubscribe on hard bounce.
  • Channel fallback: push fails, then SMS.
  • Localisation and template versioning: template per language with a version for safe rollout.

Common interview traps.

  • Marketing mail without an unsubscribe path.
  • Treating "accepted by provider" as "delivered to the user".

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Strategy per channel behind a Channel interface; the service renders once and fans out to opted-in channels.
  • Retry only transient errors, with exponential backoff (and jitter in production); park exhausted messages in a dead-letter list.
  • Fail fast on missing template variables.
  • Production shape: enqueue, then channel workers with bulkheads, timeouts and circuit breakers; dedupe by notification id.
  • Do not sleep in worker threads at scale; re-enqueue with delay.

questions.promptHtml: How do you design the notification service so adding WhatsApp later does not touch existing code, and why render the message once?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks open/closed design and that you separate rendering, delivery and retry concerns.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A Channel interface with type() and send(Message), one class per provider (Strategy). The service holds a map from channel type to implementation, renders the template once, then fans out to each channel the user opted into. Adding WhatsApp is one enum value, one class, one registration. Rendering once keeps the body identical across channels and retries.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
NotificationService
   |- TemplateEngine.render(name, vars)      once
   |- for t in wanted & user.optedIn:
         Message(t, user.addressFor(t), body)
         channels[t].send(message)           with retry, independently

The alternative, subclassing per notification type (EmailOrderShipped, SmsOrderShipped), explodes combinatorially. Business code never says new TwilioClient(); it calls the service, so swapping a provider is one class. One channel failing must not block the others, so each delivery has its own retry loop.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• A giant if (type == EMAIL) ... else if (type == SMS) in the service.
  • Retry logic copied into each channel class.
  • Forgetting user opt-in and unsubscribe (a legal requirement for marketing mail).
  • User knowing about providers.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do retries live? -> In the service (or a decorator), not in each channel.
  2. A template variable is missing? -> Fail fast; never send "Hi {{name}}".
  3. Channels need different payloads (rich push vs plain SMS)? -> Per-channel template variants, a one-way-ish change since many callers depend on the interface.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer names Strategy. The senior says where the seam is, why retry is not in the strategy, and what breaks the abstraction (very different payloads).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that hard-coded one SMS vendor had to rewrite call sites in 14 services during a vendor outage.

questions.promptHtml: Explain your retry policy for failed sends: what do you retry, how long do you wait, and what happens when attempts run out?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Naive retry loops cause outages; interviewers want to hear transient vs permanent errors, backoff, jitter and a dead-letter path.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Retry only transient errors: timeouts, 5xx and 429. Do not retry permanent ones such as an invalid phone number. Wait with exponential backoff, base times 2 to the power attempt minus one, capped, plus jitter so thousands of failures do not retry in lockstep. After the last attempt, park the message in a dead-letter queue for alerting and replay, and do not sleep after the final failure.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Attempt 1 fails -> wait 100 ms -> Attempt 2 fails -> wait 200 ms -> Attempt 3 fails -> dead letter
delay(n) = min(cap, base << (n-1)) + random(0..delay/2)

Blocking a worker thread with sleep pins it; at scale re-enqueue with a delay (SQS delay, Kafka retry topics such as retry-1m). Retries need idempotency: the user may get a duplicate SMS if the first attempt actually succeeded but timed out; pass an idempotency key where the provider supports it. Keep the delay a long and cap it to avoid shift overflow at high attempt counts.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
long delayMs(int attempt) { return Math.min(capMs, baseMs << (attempt - 1)); }
fun delayMs(attempt: Int) = minOf(capMs, baseMs shl (attempt - 1))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Retrying 400s (invalid input) three times.
  • No jitter: a provider blip makes every client retry at the same instants.
  • Sleeping after the final attempt.
  • Unbounded retries or an unbounded queue.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you replay dead letters? -> A tool or job reads the DLQ after the provider recovers; messages carry their original id.
  2. What does a circuit breaker add? -> After N consecutive failures stop calling the provider for a window and route to the retry queue.
  3. Retry budget? -> Cap retries to a fraction of total traffic so retries cannot themselves overload a struggling provider.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "retry 3 times". The senior classifies errors, adds jitter, avoids blocking threads, and names idempotency and the retry budget.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A provider blip produced a synchronised retry wave that doubled load on recovery; adding jitter flattened it.

questions.contextHtml:
Review this delivery method. In production, users who chose email and SMS get no SMS whenever the email provider is down, and the customer sometimes waits 7 seconds before the API returns.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
void notify(User u, String tpl, Map<String,String> vars, Set<ChannelType> wanted) throws Exception {
    for (ChannelType t : wanted) {
        String body = templates.render(tpl, vars);
        Channel c = channels.get(t);
        for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= 3; attempt++) {
            c.send(new Message(t, u.addressFor(t), body));   // throws on failure
            return;
        }
        Thread.sleep(2000L * 3);
    }
}
fun notify(u: User, tpl: String, vars: Map<String, String>, wanted: Set<ChannelType>) {
    for (t in wanted) {
        val body = templates.render(tpl, vars)
        for (attempt in 1..3) {
            channels.getValue(t).send(Message(t, u.addressFor(t), body))
            return
        }
        Thread.sleep(2000L * 3)
    }
}

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap it in try/catch." Never questions the return inside the loop or the missing opt-in check.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should one channel's failure affect others (no)? Are users opted in per channel? Is this on the request thread?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the endpoint's synchronous path or wrap each channel in isolation; not a data-loss issue.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (bugs found): (a) the exception from the first channel escapes the loop and aborts the rest; (b) the retry loop never retries: return after the first attempt, and an exception leaves the loop; (c) Thread.sleep is outside any failure path, always waiting; (d) body is rendered per channel inside the loop; (e) no opt-in check and no dead letter; (f) sleeps on the request thread.
  4. How I'd verify: Test with a fake channel that always throws: expect the other channel still sent, three attempts, delays recorded by an injected sleeper, and one dead-letter entry.
  5. Root cause: Control flow tangled: no per-channel try/catch, no retry structure, and orchestration mixed with delivery.
  6. Fix: Render once; for each opted-in channel call a deliver method with a try/catch inside the attempt loop, sleep only between attempts (not after the last), and add to the dead-letter list on exhaustion.
  7. Prevention: Failure-path tests with fake channels; static review rule: no Thread.sleep in request threads.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not catch Exception and swallow it silently; record it and the dead letter.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Which errors should not be retried? -> 4xx validation errors.
  • What if all three channels fail? -> Dead letter all, return a per-channel result map.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A dead email provider silently blocked SMS OTPs for 40 minutes because one exception escaped a fan-out loop.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds a try/catch around everything.
  • Hire: isolates channels, fixes the retry loop, no sleep after last.
  • Strong hire: render once, dead letter, opt-in, non-blocking path, tests with a fake sleeper.

questions.contextHtml: The service has EMAIL, SMS and PUSH. Two requests land: (1) add WhatsApp; (2) OTP messages must never wait behind a marketing blast of 5M messages, which currently shares one queue and one pool. Marketing blasts delay OTPs by up to 6 minutes at 10:00 daily.
questions.promptHtml: What changes, in which classes, and what remains untouched?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds if (type == WHATSAPP) and raises the pool size.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the OTP SLO (for example 5 seconds)? Are templates approved per channel for WhatsApp? Fallback if WhatsApp fails? Can OTP use a different provider?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Route OTP to its own queue and worker pool now; this is config, not a redesign.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) head-of-line blocking in a single queue; (b) shared provider rate limit consumed by marketing; (c) retries of failed marketing messages hogging workers.
  4. How I'd verify: Queue age per message type, pool utilisation, provider 429 counts; replay a blast in staging.
  5. Root cause: Priority classes share one queue, so a bulk class starves a critical class.
  6. Fix: Part 1: new WhatsAppChannel implements Channel, enum value, registration; service, templates and retry unchanged (open/closed). Part 2: add a priority or message class to the request, with separate queues/topics and consumer pools (bulkhead), plus per-class provider quotas; OTP path with tight timeouts and few retries.
  7. Prevention: Alert on oldest-message age per queue; load test OTP latency during a blast.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a priority queue inside one pool as the only measure (starvation, ordering complexity), separate queues are simpler. Rate-limit marketing, not OTP.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• WhatsApp needs pre-approved templates? -> TemplateEngine variant per channel, versioned.
  • Provider quota is shared? -> Reserve capacity for OTP in the limiter.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Login codes arrived minutes late each morning until marketing and OTP were given separate topics and worker groups.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: if/else and bigger pool.
  • Hire: new Strategy class, separate queue for OTP.
  • Strong hire: bulkheads, provider quotas, SLO metric by queue age.

questions.contextHtml: The retry tests for the notification service take 90 seconds in CI because they call Thread.sleep for real backoff delays (100, 200, 400 ms across 60 tests) and sometimes flake when a real HTTP call to a sandbox provider times out.
questions.promptHtml: How do you make these tests fast and deterministic, and what do you assert?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Reduce the delays in the test config" or retries with a mocking framework that hides the delay assertions.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can the service take a sleeper in its constructor? Which behaviours matter: attempt count, delays, dead letter, isolation?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Mark sandbox-calling tests as integration tests, separate them from the unit suite.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (cause of slowness and flakiness): real sleeping; real network; shared mutable state between tests.
  4. How I'd verify: Measure per-test time; run the suite with the network off; it should still pass.
  5. Root cause: Time and the provider are hidden dependencies.
  6. Fix: Inject a Sleeper (record delays instead of waiting) and use FakeChannel that fails N times.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
List<Long> slept = new ArrayList<>();
NotificationService svc = new NotificationService(List.of(email, sms, push), tpl,
        new RetryPolicy(3, 100, 1000), slept::add);
svc.notify(u, "order_shipped", vars, EnumSet.allOf(ChannelType.class));
assertEquals(List.of(100L, 200L, 100L, 200L), slept);   // email twice, sms twice; no sleep after last attempt
assertEquals(1, svc.deadLetter.size());
val slept = mutableListOf<Long>()
val svc = NotificationService(listOf(email, sms, push), render, RetryPolicy(3, 100, 1000)) { slept += it }
svc.notify(optedIn, addr, "order_shipped", vars, ChannelType.values().toSet())
assertEquals(listOf(100L, 200L, 100L, 200L), slept)
assertEquals(1, svc.deadLetter.size)

Assertions: per-channel result map, attempt counts, recorded delays, dead-letter size, template with a missing variable rejected, 50 async sends all arrive. 7. Prevention: Ban real sleeps and real network in unit tests; contract tests per provider against a sandbox, run nightly. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a global "test mode" flag in production code; inject the dependency instead.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• How to test jitter? -> Inject the random source or assert the range.
  • How to test the circuit breaker? -> A fake clock and a channel that fails K times.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A 12-minute CI run dropped to 8 seconds after replacing sleeps with a recording sleeper, and the flaky sandbox tests moved to a nightly job.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: shortens delays, keeps real calls.
  • Hire: fake channel and injected sleeper.
  • Strong hire: asserts exact delay sequence and the failure paths, separates contract tests.

questions.contextHtml:
At 18:05 the SMS provider degrades from 150 ms to 10 s responses (no errors). Within three minutes all notifications stall, including email and push. Dashboards:

thread_pool shared: active=200/200  queue=48,000 and growing
email p99 send 40 ms (provider fine)    sms p99 10,200 ms
http client: no read timeout configured (default infinite)
kafka consumer lag: 3 min -> 41 min
questions.promptHtml: Explain the failure chain, mitigate now, and fix the design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Scale the pool to 1,000." That only delays the same exhaustion.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are all channels on one pool? Are timeouts set on the HTTP client? Is there a circuit breaker? Is the queue bounded?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause or divert SMS traffic (feature flag), restart consumers with a 2 s timeout, and let email and push drain.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) shared pool exhausted by slow SMS calls (Little's law: 2,000 sends/s x 10 s = 20,000 threads needed); (b) no timeouts; (c) unbounded queue hiding the stall. Red herring: email provider, which is healthy.
  4. How I'd verify: Thread dump showing threads blocked in SMS HTTP reads; per-channel latency; active threads by channel.
  5. Root cause: No isolation (shared pool), no timeouts, no circuit breaker: one slow dependency consumed every thread.
  6. Fix: Timeouts on every provider call (for example 2 s); a bulkhead per channel (own pool or queue); circuit breaker that opens after N consecutive failures for 30 s and routes to the retry queue; bounded queues with backpressure; re-enqueue with delay rather than blocking sleeps.
  7. Prevention: Fault-injection test with a slow fake provider; alerts on oldest message age and active threads per channel.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not remove retries; I would not make the queue unbounded. A breaker may delay some deliveries; that is acceptable for isolation.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The provider is the only SMS vendor? -> Add a secondary provider with failover, still behind Channel.
  • Timeout too short for legit slow responses? -> Set from p99 plus margin and track timeout rate.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A degraded SMS vendor froze the whole notification platform for 40 minutes because HTTP calls had no read timeout.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: just scale threads.
  • Hire: timeouts, bulkhead, breaker.
  • Strong hire: Little's law math, backpressure, delayed re-enqueue, fault injection tests.

questions.contextHtml:
Customers report receiving the same "order shipped" SMS two to four times. Messages are consumed from a queue with at-least-once delivery; the SMS call takes about 3 s and the queue visibility timeout is 2 s. Excerpt:

consumer-4 11:20:01 recv id=N77 -> send SMS (provider call started)
queue      11:20:03 visibility timeout, redelivered N77
consumer-9 11:20:03 recv id=N77 -> send SMS
consumer-4 11:20:04 send OK id=N77     consumer-9 11:20:06 send OK id=N77

The business wants: no duplicate for transactional SMS, but never lose one.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and how do you fix it, given at-least-once delivery?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make the queue exactly-once." Exactly-once end-to-end is not available when the provider call is a side effect.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the provider support idempotency keys? How long can a duplicate be tolerated? Is there a notification id on every message?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise visibility timeout above worst-case processing (for example 30 s) and add a dedupe check.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) visibility timeout shorter than processing time causes redelivery; (b) producer retries enqueue the same notification twice; (c) provider retried internally. Red herring: template rendering.
  4. How I'd verify: Group logs by notification id; count deliveries; compare timeout against p99 send time (3 s vs 2 s).
  5. Root cause: At-least-once delivery plus a non-idempotent side effect.
  6. Fix: Dedupe by notificationId: Redis SET key NX EX 86400 before sending (claim); on success mark done, on failure delete the claim or let it expire so a retry is possible. Pass the id as the provider's idempotency key if supported. Extend the visibility timeout while processing (heartbeat).
  7. Prevention: Tests redelivering the same message; metric for duplicate-suppressed count; alert on redelivery rate.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The claim has a crash window (claimed, then crashed before sending: the message waits for the claim TTL). That is the price of preferring no duplicates over no losses; for OTPs prefer a duplicate over a loss.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Redis down? -> Fail open for OTPs (allow duplicates) or fail closed for marketing; decide per class.
  • Provider accepted but did not deliver? -> Track by webhook delivery status, separate from send.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A queue timeout shorter than the vendor's p99 caused thousands of duplicates daily; the visibility change plus an id-based claim cut them to near zero.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "exactly-once queue".
  • Hire: idempotency/dedupe by id and visibility timeout.
  • Strong hire: names the claim crash window, fail-open vs fail-closed per class, provider idempotency key.

questions.contextHtml: A flash sale push goes to 2M users at 12:00. Today the system sends 20,000 messages/s and FCM errors 1%. The next sale targets 20M users (10x), with the business asking that 95% of users receive the push within 2 minutes. Retries use 3 attempts with 100 ms base backoff on the worker thread.
questions.promptHtml: Do the math, find the bottlenecks, and propose the design changes.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more servers." No numbers, no thought about the provider limits or retry load.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the provider's rate limit (verify with the vendor)? Can the send be spread (time zones, segments)? Is the push idempotent per user? What is the priority vs transactional traffic?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not a live incident; protect transactional queues with separate capacity.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (bottlenecks): (a) throughput: 20M in 120 s needs about 167k sends/s (8x today); (b) provider quotas; (c) retries: 1% failure means 200k messages retrying, about 600 ms of waiting each on a blocked worker if retried inline; (d) the enqueue path and fan-out query for 20M recipients.
  4. How I'd verify: Load test with a fake provider at 200k/s; measure per-worker rate (about 150 ms each means about 6.7 sends/s/thread with blocking calls: 167k/s would need about 25,000 threads, so use async HTTP/2 batching instead); check provider quota and batch APIs (verify).
  5. Root cause of the gap: Design sized for 20k/s and for blocking calls.
  6. Fix: Partition recipients into shards (for example 200 partitions) processed in parallel by push workers; batch sends where the provider supports it; async non-blocking clients; retries re-enqueued with delay and jitter, not slept on workers; a separate topic for campaigns, rate-limited per provider; stagger the campaign by segments if the 2-minute SLO allows.
  7. Prevention: Load test every campaign tier; dashboards for send rate, retry rate, queue age; a kill switch.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: More partitions means more cost and a harder replay, but it is reversible. I would not retry inline, and I would not exceed provider quotas, which causes 429s and worsens retries.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Provider limit is 100k/s? -> The 2-minute target needs multiple credentials/projects or a relaxed SLO; negotiate or segment.
  • A user gets two pushes? -> Dedupe by (campaignId, userId).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A campaign sized for 1M users hit 12M; inline retries tied up all workers, and moving retries to delayed topics restored throughput.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "more servers".
  • Hire: does the rate math, partitions, async sends, delayed retries.
  • Strong hire: provider quotas, 429 handling, campaign isolation, per-user dedupe, load test plan.
